A 32-year-old woman was referred to the thyroid clinic with a 4-week history of flu-like symptoms, difficulty in swallowing, and pain in the neck region. On examination, she was noticed to have bilateral tremors and tenderness in the neck on palpation. Her heart rate was 84 beats/minute, regular.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FT4 | 20.5 pmol/L | 11.5–19.7 |
| FT3 | 5.5 pmol/L | 3.5–6.5 |
| TSH | 0.12 mU/L | 0.35–5.5 |

She underwent an RAIU scan (¹²³I) (see Fig. 2.3).

{{image}}

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management plan for her based on her clinical profile?**
explanation_md: The clinical profile of flu-like symptoms, neck pain, mild features of hyperthyroidism, and lack of uptake on RAIU scan is consistent with a diagnosis of subacute/de Quervains' thyroiditis. It is usually a self-limiting disease and may show a triphasic clinical course (hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, followed by a euthyroid state). The hyperthyroid state is believed to be due to destruction of thyroid follicles (due to inflammatory process) resulting in the release of preformed thyroid hormones into the circulation. Patients may need β-blockers such as propranolol for symptom relief, and anti-inflammatory agents. This stage may last for 6–8 weeks and is usually followed by a hypothyroid or euthyroid state. Anti-thyroid medications are usually not required.

stem_md:
A 36-year-old woman was referred to the thyroid clinic in view of a rapidly enlarging neck lump which she had noticed 4 weeks before. She was previously well and not on any regular medication. On examination, she had a palpable 1.5-cm thyroid nodule (firm in consistency). There was no cervical lymph node enlargement. She was referred for an urgent ultrasound of the thyroid gland.

**Which one of the following ultrasound features is suggestive of a malignant nodule?**

options.C: Isoechoic in relation to surrounding normal thyroid

explanation_md:
Ultrasound is a highly sensitive investigation to detect thyroid nodules. It can help in detecting thyroid carcinoma (especially papillary cancer). Ultrasound is typically the initial investigation of choice for patients presenting with a neck lump and can help identify the thyroid nodule suitable for FNAC.

**Table 2.17** Ultrasound features indicative of benign and malignant nodule

| Benign nodule | Malignant papillary and medullary nodule | Follicular lesions |
|---|---|---|
| Spongiform/honeycomb | Solid hypo-echoic nodule (may contain hyper-echoic foci, i.e. micro-calcification) | Hyper-echoic and homogenous with a well-defined halo (benign) |
| Purely cystic | Irregular margin | Hypo-echogenicity and loss of associated halo (associated with carcinoma) |
| Egg-shell calcification | Intra-nodular vascularity | |
| Isoechoic (or mildly hyper-echoic) | Absence of an associated halo | |
| Peripheral vascularity | 'Taller than wide' shape (i.e. AP diameter > TR diameter) | |

A 62-year-old man was referred to the thyroid clinic in view of a painless lump in his neck noticed 4 weeks before. He had not noticed any change in voice and his body weight had been stable. He had a background history of Type 2 DM (diet control) and hypertension. There was a family history of adenomatous polyposis. On examination, his BMI was 35 Kg/m². A 2.5-cm left-sided, firm thyroid nodule was palpable. The ultrasound of the thyroid nodule was reported as U3 (indeterminate). FNAC was reported as showing Thy2 cytology. He was referred for an urgent ultrasound of the thyroid gland.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management step?**
explanation_md:
Age >60 years, firmness of the nodule on palpation, and rapid growth are the clinical features in this man which increase the statistical probability of carcinoma in a thyroid nodule. In addition, obesity and a history of familial adenomatous polyposis are considered as risk factors for thyroid cancer. Although the nodule has Thy2 cytology, the index of suspicion of thyroid carcinoma remains high in view of the above mentioned clinical features and U3 (indeterminate) ultrasound features. Such patients should undergo repeat FNAC for confirmation.

**Table 2.18** Radiological classification of thyroid nodules

| U classification | Interpretation | Action |
|---|---|---|
| U1 | Normal | Discharge |
| U2 | Benign | FNAC not required (unless clinical suspicion of malignancy) |
| U3 | Indeterminate | FNAC |
| U4 | Suspicious | FNAC |
| U5 | Malignant | FNAC |

Abbreviation: FNAC: fine-needle aspiration cytology

A 63-year-old woman was referred to the endocrine clinic in view of incidentally detected focal Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) activity in the thyroid gland on PET-CT. She had undergone PET-CT as part of a diagnostic staging for pancreatic carcinoma. She had no past medical history of thyroid dysfunction and was not on any regular medication (apart from co-codamol tablets for pain relief). On examination, her pulse rate was 70 beats/minute. There were no tremors or eye signs of Graves' orbitopathy. There was no visible or palpable thyroid nodule. There was no cervical lymph node enlargement.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management approach?**
explanation_md: Nodules detected by PET-CT with focal FDG activity should be investigated with ultrasound and FNAC (unless it is metastatic disease with poor prognosis due to alternative malignancy). The risk of malignancy in such lesions is 25–50%. In contrast, diffuse uptake on FDG PET has been reported in 0.6–3.3% of the normal population.
